results.title: Monic polynomials have roots in valuation subrings of closed fields
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A monic polynomial over a valuation subring of an algebraically closed field, of nonzero degree, has a root in the subring: take a root in the field, it is integral over the subring, and valuation subrings are integrally closed.

results.title: Residue field of a valuation subring of a closed field is closed

results.summary: The residue field of a valuation subring of an algebraically closed field is algebraically closed: lift a monic irreducible polynomial to the valuation subring, take a root there, and reduce it back.

results.title: Bound on the number of ideals of bounded norm, integer threshold
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field of degree $n = [K : \mathbb{Q}]$ with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$, let $M$ be a natural number, and let $k$ be the largest natural number with $2^k \le M$, with $k = 0$ if $M = 0$. Then the number of nonzero ideals $I$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ whose absolute norm $N(I) = |\mathcal{O}_K / I|$ satisfies $N(I) \le M$ is at most $(nM)^k$.

results.title: Bound on the number of ideals of bounded norm, floor form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field of degree $n = [K : \mathbb{Q}]$ with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$, let $M$ be any real number, and let $m = \max(0, \lfloor M \rfloor)$. Let $k$ be the largest natural number with $2^k \le m$, and $k = 0$ if $m = 0$. Then the number of nonzero ideals $I$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ whose absolute norm $N(I) = |\mathcal{O}_K / I|$ satisfies $N(I) \le M$ is at most $(nm)^k$.

results.title: Bound on the number of ideals of bounded norm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a number field of degree $n = [K : \mathbb{Q}]$ with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$, and let $M > 0$ be a real number. The number of nonzero ideals $I$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ whose absolute norm $N(I) = |\mathcal{O}_K / I|$ satisfies $N(I) \le M$ is at most $(nM)^{\log_2 M}$, where the exponent $\log_2 M$ is a real number.

results.title: Left-hand indices of the cyclic sum formula
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Integrality of the Fuss–Catalan numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $a \ge 2$ and $n \ge 1$, the integer $(a-1)n + 1$ divides the binomial coefficient $\binom{an}{n}$. Hence the Fuss–Catalan number $\frac{1}{(a-1)n+1}\binom{an}{n}$ is an integer.

results.title: Fuss–Catalan numbers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $k \ge 1$ (the chord arity) and $m$, the Fuss–Catalan number is the natural-number quotient of $\binom{km}{m}$ by $(k-1)m+1$, that is $\lfloor \binom{km}{m} / ((k-1)m+1) \rfloor$.

results.title: Prime divisibility of generalized Catalan numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and $n$ a natural number. Then $p$ divides the generalized Catalan number $\frac{1}{(p-1)n+1}\binom{pn}{n}$ (an integer) if and only if $n$ is not of the form $\frac{p^k-1}{p-1}$ for any natural number $k$.

results.title: Generalized Fuss–Catalan number

results.title: Integer unit cube
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$, the integer unit cube at $v$ is the half-open cube $Q_v = \prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, the set of $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $v_i \le x_i < v_i + 1$ for every coordinate $i$.

results.title: Membership in an integer unit cube
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $x$ lies in the integer unit cube at $v$ if and only if $v_i \le x_i < v_i + 1$ for every coordinate $i$.

results.title: Outer cube set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and a real number $t$, the outer cube set of $S$ at scale $t$ is the set of $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ such that $(x_1/t, \dots, x_n/t) \in S$ for some $x$ in the integer unit cube $Q_v = \prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1)$. For $t > 0$ these are the $v$ with $Q_v$ meeting $tS$; for $t = 0$ the division is read as $x_i/0 = 0$.

results.title: Membership in the outer cube set

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and every real $t$, the inner cube set of $S$ at scale $t$ is contained in the outer cube set of $S$ at scale $t$.

results.title: Finiteness of the outer cube set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is bounded and $t > 0$, then the outer cube set of $S$ at scale $t$, the set of $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ whose integer unit cube $\prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1)$ meets $tS$, is finite.

results.title: Cubical measure sandwich
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be bounded, let $t > 0$, and let $\mathrm{vol}(S)$ be the Lebesgue (outer) measure of $S$, which is finite. For $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ let $Q_v = \prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1)$. Let $I$ be the inner cube set of $S$ at scale $t$, the $v$ with $Q_v \subseteq tS$, and $O$ the outer cube set, the $v$ with $Q_v$ meeting $tS$. Then $|I| \le \mathrm{vol}(S)\, t^n \le |O|$.

results.title: The standard integer lattice
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, the standard integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is the $\mathbb{Z}$-submodule of $\mathbb{R}^d$ (the real-valued functions on $\{0, \dots, d-1\}$) spanned by the standard basis vectors $e_0, \dots, e_{d-1}$.

results.title: Membership in the standard lattice
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, a vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ lies in the standard lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$, the integer span of the standard basis vectors of $\mathbb{R}^d$, exactly when every coordinate $x_i$ of $x$ is an integer.

results.title: Lattice points in a dilate
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $t$, this is the set $(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$.

results.title: Lattice-point count of a real dilate
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $t$, this is the number of elements of the set $(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$, where an infinite set is assigned the value $0$.

results.title: Translated lattice-point set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, a real $t$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the translated lattice-point set is $((t \cdot P) + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$, the set of points of the standard integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $t \cdot P$ translated by $x$.

results.title: Translated lattice-point count for arbitrary sets
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, a real $t$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the translated lattice-point count is the number of elements of the translated lattice-point set $((t \cdot P) + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$, taken to be $0$ when this set is infinite.

results.title: Lattice points in a positive dilate
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $t > 0$, this is the set $(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$.

results.title: Lattice-point enumerator
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, a bounded set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $t > 0$, the lattice-point enumerator $L_P(t)$ is the number of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$, that is, $L_P(t) = |(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d|$.

results.title: Translated lattice-point set at a positive dilation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $d \in \mathbb{N}$, a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, a real $t > 0$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, this is the set $((t \cdot P) + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the standard integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $t \cdot P$ translated by $x$. No boundedness of $P$ is assumed.

results.title: Translated lattice-point enumerator of a bounded set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$, let $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded set, let $t > 0$ be real and let $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$. The translated lattice-point enumerator is $F_{t,P}(x) = |((t \cdot P) + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d|$, the number of points of the standard integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $t \cdot P$ translated by $x$.

results.title: The origin is a lattice point
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $d \in \mathbb{N}$, the origin of $\mathbb{R}^d$ lies in the standard integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$.

results.title: The lattice-point count of the empty set vanishes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $d$ and every real number $t$, the lattice-point count of the empty set $\emptyset \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ at the dilate $t$ is $0$.

results.title: The translated lattice-point count of the empty set is zero
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $d \in \mathbb{N}$, every real $t$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the translated lattice-point count $|((t \cdot \emptyset) + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d|$ is $0$.

results.title: Finiteness of the lattice points in a dilate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, a bounded set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and any real number $t$, the set $(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$ is finite.

results.title: Finiteness of the lattice points in a positive dilate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, a bounded set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and a real number $t > 0$, the set $(tP) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the dilate $tP = \{tp : p \in P\}$ is finite.

results.title: Finiteness of the lattice points in a translated dilate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, a bounded set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, any real number $t$ and a vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the set $(tP + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the translated dilate $tP + x = \{tp + x : p \in P\}$ is finite.

results.title: Finiteness of the lattice points in a translated positive dilate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, a bounded set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, a real number $t > 0$ and a vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the set $(tP + x) \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ of points of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ in the translated dilate $tP + x = \{tp + x : p \in P\}$ is finite.

results.title: The unit cube
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $d$, the closed unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ is the set of points $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $0 \le x_i \le 1$ for every coordinate $i$.

results.title: Lipschitz parametrizable sets
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $X$ be a metric space and $d$ a natural number. A set $B \subseteq X$ is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable if there are a natural number $n$ (possibly $0$) and Lipschitz maps $f_1, \dots, f_n : [0, 1]^d \to X$ out of the closed unit cube $[0, 1]^d \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ such that $B$ equals the union of their images, $B = f_1([0, 1]^d) \cup \dots \cup f_n([0, 1]^d)$.

results.title: The origin lies in the unit cube
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $d$, the origin of $\mathbb{R}^d$ lies in the closed unit cube $[0, 1]^d$.

results.title: The empty set is Lipschitz parametrizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $X$ be a metric space. For every natural number $d$, the empty subset of $X$ is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable, via the empty family of maps.

results.title: Singletons are Lipschitz parametrizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $X$ be a metric space. For every natural number $d$ and every point $x \in X$, the set $\lbrace x \rbrace$ is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable, via a single constant map.

results.title: Finsets are Lipschitz parametrizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $X$ be a metric space and $d$ a natural number. Every finite set $s$ of points of $X$, given as a finset, is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable.

results.title: Finite sets are Lipschitz parametrizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $X$ be a metric space. Every finite set $B \subseteq X$ is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable for every natural number $d$.

results.title: Lipschitz images of Lipschitz parametrizable sets
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $X$ and $Y$ be metric spaces, let $d$ be a natural number and let $f : X \to Y$ be a Lipschitz map. If a set $B \subseteq X$ is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable, then its image $f(B) \subseteq Y$ is $d$-Lipschitz parametrizable.

results.title: Integer cube set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $f$ be a map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $t$ be a real number. The integer cube set of $f$ at scale $t$ is the set of integer vectors $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ for which some point $y$ of the unit cube satisfies $v_i \le t f(y)_i < v_i + 1$ for every coordinate $i$, that is, the set of integer vectors whose half-open unit cube $\prod_i [v_i, v_i + 1)$ meets the dilate $t \cdot f([0, 1]^d)$.

results.title: Membership in the integer cube set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$, let $t$ be a real number and let $v \in \mathbb{Z}^n$. Then $v$ belongs to the integer cube set of $f$ at scale $t$ if and only if some point $y$ of the unit cube satisfies $v_i \le t f(y)_i < v_i + 1$ for every coordinate $i$.

results.title: Floor differences are bounded by a ceiling
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For real numbers $a$, $b$ and $D$ with $|a - b| \le D$, the integers $\lfloor a \rfloor$ and $\lfloor b \rfloor$ satisfy $|\lfloor a \rfloor - \lfloor b \rfloor| \le \lceil D \rceil$.

results.title: Dilated Lipschitz maps vary by at most $K$ on cells of size $1/T$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K \ge 0$, let $f$ be a $K$-Lipschitz map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$, both carrying the sup distance, and let $t$ and $T$ be real numbers with $0 < t \le T$. If $y$ and $y'$ are points of the unit cube at distance at most $1/T$, then $|t f(y)_i - t f(y')_i| \le K$ for every coordinate $i$.

results.title: Counting integer cubes met by a dilated Lipschitz image
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d$ and $n$ be natural numbers, let $K \ge 0$, and let $f$ be a $K$-Lipschitz map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$, both carrying the sup distance. For every real $t \ge 1$, the cardinality of the integer cube set of $f$ at scale $t$, taken as a natural number, is at most $\lceil t \rceil^d \, (2 \lceil K \sqrt{d} \rceil + 3)^n$.

results.title: Dilated Lipschitz images meet finitely many integer cubes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d$ and $n$ be natural numbers, let $K \ge 0$, and let $f$ be a $K$-Lipschitz map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$, both carrying the sup distance. For every real $t \ge 1$, the integer cube set of $f$ at scale $t$ is finite.

results.title: Dilated Lipschitz images meet $O(t^d)$ integer cubes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d$ and $n$ be natural numbers, let $K \ge 0$, and let $f$ be a $K$-Lipschitz map from the unit cube $[0, 1]^d$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$, both carrying the sup distance. Then there is a real number $C > 0$ such that for every real $t \ge 1$, the cardinality of the integer cube set of $f$ at scale $t$, taken as a natural number, is at most $C t^d$.

results.title: Red-black node colors
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The colors of red-black tree nodes are the two values red and black.

results.title: Red-black tree data type
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A red-black tree with keys in a type $\alpha$ is either empty or a node consisting of a color (red or black), a left subtree, a key in $\alpha$, and a right subtree.

results.title: Color erasure
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The color erasure of a red-black tree is the binary tree obtained by forgetting the node colors: the empty tree goes to the empty binary tree, and a node with key $k$ and subtrees $l$ and $r$ goes to the binary-tree node with key $k$ whose subtrees are the color erasures of $l$ and $r$.

results.title: Membership in a red-black tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An element $x$ is a member of a red-black tree $t$ when $x$ is a member of the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its colors, that is, when $x$ equals the key of some node of $t$.

results.title: Inorder traversal onto a suffix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a red-black tree $t$ and a list $s$, this is the accumulator form of the binary-search-tree inorder traversal applied to the color erasure of $t$: for the empty tree it returns $s$, and for a node with key $k$ and subtrees $l$ and $r$ it returns the result for $l$ with suffix the list $k$ followed by $u$, where $u$ is the result for $r$ with suffix $s$.

results.title: Inorder traversal of a red-black tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The inorder traversal of a red-black tree $t$ is the binary-search-tree inorder traversal of the color erasure of $t$, computed in linear time with an accumulator starting from the empty list. It lists the keys of $t$ from left to right: the empty tree gives the empty list, and a node with key $k$ and subtrees $l$ and $r$ gives the traversal of $l$, then $k$, then the traversal of $r$.

results.title: Predicate holding at every key of a red-black tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and a red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ when $p$ holds at every key of the binary search tree obtained from $t$ by erasing colors.

results.title: Ordered red-black tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ is ordered when, at every node with key $k$, every key $y$ in the left subtree satisfies $y < k$ and every key $z$ in the right subtree satisfies $k < z$.

results.title: Red-black membership is membership in the underlying binary tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every red-black tree $t$ and every $x$, $x$ is a member of $t$ if and only if $x$ is a member of the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its colors.

results.title: All keys of a red-black tree via its color erasure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and every red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ if and only if $p$ holds at every key of the binary search tree obtained from $t$ by erasing colors. This holds by definition.

results.title: A red-black tree is ordered exactly when its underlying binary tree is
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For keys with a relation $<$, a red-black tree $t$ is ordered if and only if the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its colors is an ordered binary search tree.

results.title: Inorder traversal ignores colors
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every red-black tree $t$, the inorder traversal of $t$ equals the binary-search-tree inorder traversal of the color erasure of $t$; this holds by definition.

results.title: Root color
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The root color of a red-black tree is the color of its root node; the empty tree has root color black.

results.title: Red property of red-black trees
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A red-black tree satisfies the red property when no red node has a red child, where empty subtrees count as black.

results.title: Red invariant away from the root
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A red-black tree satisfies the relaxed red invariant when it is empty, or when its left and right subtrees both satisfy the red invariant (no red node has a red child). The root itself is unconstrained, so a red root may have a red child.

results.title: Black height
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The black height of a red-black tree is the number of black nodes on its leftmost root-to-leaf path, counting the empty leaf as one black node: the empty tree has black height $1$, a red node has the black height of its left subtree, and a black node has the black height of its left subtree plus $1$.

results.title: Black-height balanced red-black tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A red-black tree is balanced when every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes. Recursively: the empty tree is balanced, and a node is balanced when both of its subtrees are balanced and have the same black height (the number of black nodes on the leftmost root-to-leaf path, counting the leaf).

results.title: Valid red-black tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ is valid when it is ordered, satisfies the red property (no red node has a red child), is balanced (every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes), and its root is black, where the empty tree counts as black.

results.title: Search in a red-black tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Searching a red-black tree over a linearly ordered type for a key $x$ returns a Boolean, ignoring colors: the empty tree gives false, and at a node with key $k$ the search continues in the left subtree if $x < k$, continues in the right subtree if $k < x$, and returns true otherwise.

results.title: Unchecked red-black insertion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, the unchecked insertion of $x$ into a red-black tree is defined by recursion on the tree. Inserting $x$ into the empty tree gives a red node with key $x$ and two empty subtrees. results.title: Blackening the root
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Recoloring the root of a red-black tree black leaves the empty tree unchanged and turns a node with any color, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ into the black node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$.

results.title: Recoloring the root black does not change the color erasure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every red-black tree $t$, the color erasure of the tree obtained from $t$ by recoloring its root black (the empty tree is left unchanged) equals the color erasure of $t$.

results.title: Red-black tree insertion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, inserting $x$ into a red-black tree $t$ gives the unchecked insertion of $x$ into $t$ with its root recolored black.

results.title: Red-black tree from a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The red-black tree built from a list over a linearly ordered type inserts the elements of the list into the empty tree from right to left: the empty list gives the empty tree, and a list with head $x$ and tail $xs$ gives the insertion of $x$ into the tree built from $xs$.

results.title: All keys versus members of a red-black tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and every red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ if and only if $p(x)$ holds for every $x \in \alpha$ that is a (structural) member of $t$.

results.title: Membership in the inorder traversal of a red-black tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every red-black tree $t$ and every $x$, $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of $t$ if and only if $x$ is a member of $t$.

results.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered red-black tree is strictly increasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, if a red-black tree $t$ is ordered, then every entry of the inorder traversal of $t$ is strictly smaller than every later entry.

results.title: Membership after insertion into a red-black tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, a key $y$ is a member of the red-black tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ is a member of $t$.

results.title: Red-black insertion preserves the search-tree order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$. If $t$ is ordered (at every node with key $k$, every key in the left subtree is less than $k$ and every key in the right subtree is greater than $k$), then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is ordered.

results.title: Red-black insertion preserves the red property
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$. If no red node of $t$ has a red child, then no red node of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ has a red child.

results.title: Red-black insertion preserves black-height balance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If a red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ is balanced (every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes), then for every $x \in \alpha$ the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is balanced.

results.title: Insertion raises the black height by at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ and every $x \in \alpha$, the black height of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ equals either the black height of $t$ or the black height of $t$ plus one.

results.title: Red-black insertion yields a valid tree from the invariants
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, satisfies the red property (no red node has a red child), and is balanced (every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes). Then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is valid.

results.title: Red-black insertion preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $x \in \alpha$. If $t$ is a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$, then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is also valid.

results.title: Search in an ordered red-black tree is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a red-black tree over a linearly ordered type that is ordered (every left key is smaller and every right key larger, recursively). Then for every key $x$, the search for $x$ in $t$ returns true if and only if $x$ is a key of some node of $t$.

results.title: Ordered red-black trees have duplicate-free inorder traversals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a red-black tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type that is ordered (every left key is smaller and every right key larger, recursively), the inorder traversal of $t$ contains no key twice.

results.title: The empty red-black tree is valid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every type $\alpha$ with a relation $<$, the empty red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ is a valid red-black tree.

results.title: Red-black trees built from a list are valid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every list $l$ of elements of $\alpha$, the red-black tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting the elements of $l$ one at a time, from the last to the first, is valid.

results.title: Membership in a red-black tree built from a list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type and every list $xs$, a key $x$ is a member of the red-black tree built from $xs$ by successive insertion if and only if $x$ occurs in $xs$.

results.title: Splicing two red-black trees
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The splice of a red-black tree $t$ with a red-black tree $s$ is defined by recursion on $t$. The splice of the empty tree with $s$ is $s$. The splice of the node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ with $s$ is the node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree the splice of $r$ with $s$.

results.title: Unbalanced red-black tree deletion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, unbalanced deletion of $x$ from a red-black tree is defined by recursion on the tree. The empty tree stays empty. At a node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the result is the node with color $c$, left subtree the unbalanced deletion of $x$ from $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$; if $k < x$, it is the node with color $c$, left…

results.title: Rebuilding a red-black tree from its keys
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, the rebuild of a red-black tree $t$ is the tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting the keys of the inorder traversal of $t$ one at a time with Okasaki insertion, starting from the last key.

results.title: Red-black tree deletion by rebuilding
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and a red-black tree $t$, deleting $x$ from $t$ by rebuilding first forms the unbalanced deletion of $x$ from $t$, then rebalances it: starting from the empty tree, it inserts the keys of the inorder traversal of that tree one at a time, from the last key to the first.

results.title: Membership in a splice
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For red-black trees $t$ and $s$ with keys of any type, a key $x$ belongs to the splice of $t$ with $s$ if and only if $x$ belongs to $t$ or $x$ belongs to $s$.

results.title: Inorder traversal of a splice
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For red-black trees $t$ and $s$ with keys of any type, the inorder traversal of the splice of $t$ with $s$ is the inorder traversal of $t$ followed by the inorder traversal of $s$.

results.title: Joining separated ordered trees preserves order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $<$ be a relation on the keys, and let $L$ and $R$ be red-black trees that are ordered for $<$ such that $a < b$ for every key $a$ of $L$ and every key $b$ of $R$. Then the join of $L$ and $R$, obtained by putting $R$ in place of the empty right subtree of the rightmost node of $L$ (or $R$ itself if $L$ is empty) and keeping all colors, is ordered.

results.title: Membership after deletion by rebuilding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be keys of a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then $y$ belongs to the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding if and only if $y$ belongs to $t$ and $y \ne x$.

results.title: The deleted key is absent after deletion by rebuilding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then $x$ does not belong to the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding.

results.title: Inorder traversal after deletion by rebuilding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then the inorder traversal of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (it is unchanged if $x$ does not occur).

results.title: Red-black deletion yields a valid red-black tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every linearly ordered key type, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is a valid red-black tree: it is ordered, no red node has a red child, every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes, and its root is black (the empty tree counts as black). No hypothesis on $t$ is needed.

results.title: Red-black deletion yields an ordered tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every linearly ordered key type, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is ordered: at every node, all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller than the node's key and all keys in the right subtree are strictly larger. No hypothesis on $t$ is needed.

results.title: Red-black deletion yields a tree with no red-red edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every linearly ordered key type, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ satisfies the red invariant: no red node has a red child. No hypothesis on $t$ is needed.

results.title: Deletion by rebuilding is black-height balanced
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every linearly ordered type of keys, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, with no hypothesis on $t$, the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is black-height balanced.

results.title: Deletion by rebuilding gives a black root
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every linearly ordered type of keys, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, with no hypothesis on $t$, the root of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is black, where the empty tree counts as having a black root.

results.title: Extended root colors
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: An extended color is one of three values: red, black or double black.

results.title: Trees with a possibly double-black root
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A tree with a possibly double-black root over a type $\alpha$ is one of the following: a genuine red-black tree over $\alpha$; the double-black empty tree; or a double-black node consisting of a left subtree, a key in $\alpha$ and a right subtree, where both subtrees are genuine red-black trees. Hence a double black can occur only at the root.

results.title: Inorder traversal of a possibly double-black tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The inorder traversal of a red-black tree whose root may be double black ignores the double-black mark: a genuine tree gives its inorder traversal, the double-black empty tree gives the empty list, and a double-black node with left child $l$, key $k$ and right child $r$ gives the inorder traversal of $l$, followed by $k$, followed by the inorder traversal of $r$.

results.title: Black height of a possibly double-black tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The black height of a genuine red-black tree is its usual black height. The double-black empty tree has black height $2$, and a double-black node with left subtree $L$ has black height $h(L) + 2$, where $h(L)$ is the usual black height of $L$. Thus a double-black root counts as two black nodes, where the usual black height counts the empty tree as one.

results.title: Black-height balance of a possibly double-black tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A tree whose root may be double black is balanced when it is a genuine red-black tree that is balanced, when it is the double-black empty tree, or when it is a double-black node whose left and right subtrees are both balanced and have the same black height.

results.title: Red invariant for trees with a possibly double-black root
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A tree whose root may be double black satisfies the red invariant in the following cases: a genuine red-black tree satisfies it when it satisfies the usual red invariant (no red node has a red child); the double-black empty tree always satisfies it; and a double-black node with left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$ satisfies it when both $l$ and $r$ satisfy the usual red invariant.

results.title: Extended root color
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The extended color of a tree whose root may be double black is the color of its root, red or black, when it is a genuine red-black tree, where the empty tree counts as black; it is double black for the double-black empty tree and for every double-black node.

results.title: Adding a black to the root
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Add one black to the root of a red-black tree, producing a tree whose root may be double black: the empty tree becomes the double-black empty tree, a red root becomes black, and a black root becomes double black.

results.title: Recoloring the root black
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a red-black tree $t$, this is the tree obtained from $t$ by coloring its root black: the empty tree stays empty, and a node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$, of either color, becomes the black node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$.

results.title: Absorbing a double-black root
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Blackening sends a tree whose root may be double black to a genuine red-black tree by changing only its root: a genuine tree has its root recolored black (the empty tree stays empty), the double-black empty tree becomes the empty tree, and a double-black node becomes the black node with the same subtrees and key.

results.title: Leftmost key of a red-black tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a red-black tree $t$ over a type $\alpha$, the leftmost key of $t$ is either a key in $\alpha$ or undefined. It is undefined when $t$ is empty. When $t$ is a node, of either color, with left subtree $l$ and key $k$, it is the leftmost key of $l$ if that is defined, and $k$ otherwise. Hence the leftmost key is defined exactly when $t$ is nonempty.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write $\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ for red and black, and $N(c, T, y, T')$ for the node of color $c$ with left subtree $T$, key $y$ and right subtree $T'$. Given a color $c$, a tree $S$, a key $k$ and a tree $D$, the right repair returns a tree whose root may be double black, by the first case that applies. results.title: Rebalancing after deletion from the left subtree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $c$ be a color, $L$ a tree whose root may be double black, $k$ a key and $R$ a red-black tree. If $L$ is a genuine red-black tree, the result is the genuine node with color $c$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. Otherwise the double black of $L$ is absorbed first: a double-black empty tree becomes the empty tree, and a double-black node becomes the black node with the same children and key. The…

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $c$ be a color, $L$ a red-black tree, $k$ a key and $R$ a tree whose root may be double black. If $R$ is a genuine red-black tree, the result is the genuine node with color $c$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. Otherwise the double black of $R$ is absorbed first: a double-black empty tree becomes the empty tree, and a double-black node becomes the black node with the same children and key. The…

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, deleting $x$ from a red-black tree returns a tree whose root may be double black, by recursion on the tree. The empty tree gives the empty tree. At a node of color $c$ with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the result is the left reassembly of color $c$, the deletion of $x$ from $l$, key $k$ and $r$; if $k < x$, it is the right reassembly of color…

results.title: Red-black tree deletion by the double-black method
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and a red-black tree $t$, deleting $x$ from $t$ runs the double-black deletion of $x$ from $t$, which returns a tree whose root may be double black, and then absorbs a remaining double black at the root and recolors the root black.

results.title: Double-black deletion erases the key from the inorder traversal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and an ordered red-black tree $t$, the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (unchanged if $x$ does not occur).

results.title: Keys after double-black deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ of a linearly ordered type and an ordered red-black tree $t$, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method if and only if $y$ is a key of $t$ and $y \ne x$.

results.title: The deleted key is absent after double-black deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, that is, at every node all keys of the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys of the right subtree are strictly larger than the node's key. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the key $x$ does not occur in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method.

results.title: Double-black deletion preserves the search-tree order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, that is, at every node all keys of the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys of the right subtree are strictly larger than the node's key. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is again ordered.

results.title: Double-black deletion yields a valid tree from the structural invariants
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, satisfies the red invariant (no red node has a red child), and is black-height balanced (all root-to-leaf paths contain the same number of black nodes). Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is a valid red-black tree.

results.title: Double-black deletion preserves validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$: it is ordered, satisfies the red invariant, is black-height balanced, and has a black root. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is again a valid red-black tree.

results.title: Double-black deletion from a valid tree keeps the red invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$: it is ordered, satisfies the red invariant, is black-height balanced, and has a black root. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method satisfies the red invariant: no red node has a red child.

results.title: Double-black deletion keeps a valid tree balanced
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $T$ a valid red-black tree over $\alpha$. Then the tree obtained from $T$ by double-black deletion of $x$ is balanced.

results.title: Double-black deletion leaves a black root
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and every red-black tree $t$, valid or not, the root of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is black, where the empty tree counts as black.

results.title: Black height after double-black deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, $T$ a valid red-black tree over $\alpha$, and $T'$ the tree obtained from $T$ by double-black deletion of $x$. Then the black height of $T'$ either equals the black height of $T$ or is one less than it.

results.title: Huffman tree
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A Huffman tree over an alphabet $\alpha$ is either a leaf, which carries a symbol $a \in \alpha$ and a natural-number weight $w$, or a fork, which joins a left and a right Huffman tree over $\alpha$.

results.title: Weighted leaves of a Huffman tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The list of pairs $(s, w)$, one for each leaf of a Huffman tree, where $s$ is the symbol and $w$ the weight at that leaf, read from left to right.

results.title: List of leaf symbols of a Huffman tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The list of the symbols at the leaves of a Huffman tree, read from left to right, with one entry per leaf.

results.title: Total weight of a Huffman tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The sum of the weights at all leaves of a Huffman tree, counted once per leaf.

results.title: Weighted path length
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The weighted path length of a Huffman tree is defined recursively: a single leaf has weighted path length $0$, and the tree with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ has weighted path length equal to the weighted path length of $L$ plus that of $R$ plus the total weight of $L$ plus the total weight of $R$.

results.title: Weighted path length of a merged tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For Huffman trees $L$ and $R$, the weighted path length of the tree with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ equals the weighted path length of $L$ plus the weighted path length of $R$ plus the total weight of $L$ plus the total weight of $R$.

results.title: Encoded length of a coding tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The encoded length of a leaf of weight $w$ is $w$ (its lone symbol receives a one-bit codeword). The encoded length of the tree with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ is $P(L) + P(R) + W(L) + W(R)$, where $P$ is the weighted path length and $W$ the total weight; this is the weighted path length of that tree.

results.title: Encoded length of a fork
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For any two coding trees $L$ and $R$, the encoded length of the tree with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ equals its weighted path length.

results.title: Root-to-leaf path code
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Huffman tree $T$ and a symbol $s$, the path code of $s$ in $T$ records the edges on the path from the root of $T$ to the leftmost leaf labelled $s$, writing false for a left edge and true for a right edge. If $T$ is a single leaf labelled $s$, the path code is empty; if no leaf of $T$ is labelled $s$, there is no path code.

results.title: Decoding a bit string
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $T$ be a Huffman tree. Decoding the empty bit string with $T$ returns the empty sequence of symbols. results.title: Huffman encoding of a message
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a coding tree $T$, the empty message encodes to the empty bit string, and a message $s_1 s_2 \cdots s_n$ encodes to the concatenation, in order, of the codewords of $s_1, \dots, s_n$ in $T$. If some $s_i$ has no codeword in $T$, the message has no encoding.

results.title: Type of leaf symbols of a Huffman tree
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a Huffman tree $T$ over an alphabet $\alpha$, the type of leaf symbols of $T$ is the subtype of those $a \in \alpha$ that occur in the list of leaf symbols of $T$.

results.title: Codeword of a leaf symbol
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Huffman tree $T$ and a symbol $s$ occurring at a leaf of $T$, the codeword of $s$ is the word that the codeword lookup of $T$ returns for $s$, or the empty word if the lookup fails.

results.title: Every leaf symbol has a codeword
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a Huffman tree and $s$ a symbol occurring at a leaf of $T$. Then the codeword lookup of $s$ in $T$ succeeds.

results.title: Codeword lookup agrees with the leaf code
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a Huffman tree and $s$ a symbol occurring at a leaf of $T$. Then the codeword lookup of $s$ in $T$ succeeds and returns the codeword of $s$ as a leaf symbol of $T$.

results.title: Huffman tree codes are prefix-free
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Huffman tree $T$, the codeword map on the symbols occurring as leaves of $T$ is prefix-free: if $a$ and $b$ are distinct leaf symbols of $T$, then the codeword of $a$ is not a prefix of the codeword of $b$.

results.title: Decoding inverts the leaf code
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a Huffman tree and let $s_1, \dots, s_n$ ($n \ge 0$) be symbols occurring at leaves of $T$, with codewords $c(s_1), \dots, c(s_n)$ as leaf symbols of $T$. Decoding the concatenation $c(s_1) c(s_2) \cdots c(s_n)$ with $T$ succeeds and returns the sequence $s_1, \dots, s_n$.

results.title: Encoding concatenates leaf codewords
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a Huffman tree and let $s_1, \dots, s_n$ ($n \ge 0$) be symbols occurring at leaves of $T$, with codewords $c(s_1), \dots, c(s_n)$ as leaf symbols of $T$. Encoding $s_1, \dots, s_n$ with $T$ succeeds and returns the concatenation $c(s_1) c(s_2) \cdots c(s_n)$.

results.title: Decoding inverts encoding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a Huffman tree and let $s_1, \dots, s_n$ ($n \ge 0$) be symbols occurring at leaves of $T$. Encoding $s_1, \dots, s_n$ with $T$ and then decoding the resulting bit string with $T$, failing if the encoding fails, returns $s_1, \dots, s_n$. In particular, the encoding succeeds.

results.title: A symbol has a path code exactly when it labels a leaf
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a Huffman tree $T$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality and a symbol $a \in \alpha$, the root-to-leaf path code of $a$ in $T$ is undefined exactly when $a$ is not among the leaf symbols of $T$.

results.title: Weighted path length as a sum over leaves
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a Huffman tree whose leaf symbols are pairwise distinct. Then the weighted path length of $T$ equals the sum, over the leaves of $T$ with symbol $s$ and weight $w$, of $w$ times the length of the root-to-leaf path of $s$ in $T$ (the depth of that leaf, with the root at depth zero).

results.title: Encoded length is the total weighted codeword length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a coding tree whose leaf symbols are pairwise distinct. For a symbol $s$, let $\ell(s)$ be the length of the codeword of $s$ in $T$, or $0$ if $s$ has no codeword. Then the encoded length of $T$ equals $\sum_{(s, w)} w \cdot \ell(s)$, the sum over the weighted leaves $(s, w)$ of $T$.

results.title: Huffman priority
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A Huffman priority is a pair $(w, s)$ of natural numbers: a weight $w$ and a serial number $s$.

results.title: Huffman work item
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A work item over an alphabet $\alpha$ pairs a Huffman priority, that is, a natural-number weight and a natural-number serial, with a Huffman tree over $\alpha$.

results.title: Result of a two-minimum extraction
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A record consisting of two Huffman priorities, the first and the second, together with a binary min-heap of Huffman priorities, the rest.

results.title: Extracting two minima from a Huffman heap
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a binary min-heap $h$ of Huffman priorities, extract the minimum of $h$, obtaining a priority $p_1$ and a heap $h_1$, then extract the minimum of $h_1$, obtaining a priority $p_2$ and a heap $h_2$. The result is the triple $(p_1, p_2, h_2)$; if either extraction meets an empty heap, there is no result.

results.title: Extracting two minima preserves the heap's elements
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If extracting two minima from a binary min-heap $h$ of Huffman priorities succeeds with first priority $p_1$, second priority $p_2$ and remaining heap $h'$, then the multiset of elements of $h$ equals the multiset of elements of $h'$ with $p_1$ and $p_2$ added, counted with multiplicity.

results.title: Two-minimum extraction is greedy
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Order Huffman priorities lexicographically by weight and then serial number. If extracting two minima from a binary min-heap $h$ of Huffman priorities succeeds with first priority $p_1$, second priority $p_2$ and remaining heap $h'$, then $p_1 \le q$ for every element $q$ of $h$, and $p_2 \le q$ for every $q$ that is $p_2$ or an element of $h'$.

results.title: Work forest of a table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a table $T$ whose cells each hold at most one work item, the work forest of $T$ is the list of the work items held in the cells of $T$, in increasing cell order; empty cells are skipped.

results.title: Removing a work item by serial
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a serial number $s$ and a table $t$ of optional Huffman work items, look up the entry of $t$ at index $s$. If that entry is a work item whose serial number is $s$, the result is its tree together with the table obtained from $t$ by emptying the entry at $s$; otherwise (the index is out of bounds, the entry is empty, or it holds an item with a different serial number) the removal fails.

results.title: Weighted leaves of a Huffman work forest
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The weighted leaves of a list of Huffman work items are the concatenation, in list order, of the weighted leaves of the items' trees.

results.title: Removing a serial removes one work item from the forest
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a table of optional Huffman work items, and call the list of work items present in a table its work forest. If removing serial number $s$ from $t$ succeeds and returns a tree $T$ and an updated table $t'$, then there is a work item $w$ with tree $T$ and serial number $s$ such that $w$ followed by the work forest of $t'$ is a permutation of the work forest of $t$.

results.title: Removing a serial preserves the table size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a table of optional Huffman work items. If removing serial number $s$ from $t$ succeeds and returns a tree together with an updated table $t'$, then $t'$ has the same size as $t$.

results.title: Removing a serial leaves the other table entries unchanged
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a table of optional Huffman work items. If removing serial number $s$ from $t$ succeeds and returns a tree together with an updated table $t'$, then for every index $j \ne s$ the entry of $t'$ at $j$ equals the entry of $t$ at $j$ (both are absent when $j$ is out of bounds).

results.title: A stored work item can be removed by its serial
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a table of optional Huffman work items and let $w$ be a work item with serial number $s$. If the entry of $t$ at index $s$ is $w$, then removing serial $s$ from $t$ succeeds and returns the tree of $w$ together with an updated table.

results.title: Numbered leaf work items
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a starting serial number $s$ and a list of pairs $(a_0, w_0), \dots, (a_{k-1}, w_{k-1})$ of symbols and natural-number weights, this is the list of $k$ Huffman work items whose $i$-th entry has priority (weight $w_i$, serial $s + i$) and whose tree is the leaf with symbol $a_i$ and weight $w_i$.

results.title: Initial Huffman forest
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list of pairs $(a_0, w_0), \dots, (a_{k-1}, w_{k-1})$ of symbols and natural-number weights, the initial forest is the list of $k$ Huffman work items whose $i$-th entry has priority (weight $w_i$, serial $i$) and whose tree is the leaf with symbol $a_i$ and weight $w_i$.

results.title: Initial Huffman table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list of $k$ pairs $(a_0, w_0), \dots, (a_{k-1}, w_{k-1})$ of symbols and natural-number weights, the initial table is the array of length $k$ of optional Huffman work items whose cell $i$ is present and holds the work item with priority (weight $w_i$, serial $i$) and tree the leaf with symbol $a_i$ and weight $w_i$; that is, it is the initial Huffman forest with every entry marked present.

results.title: The initial table holds the initial forest
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list of weighted symbols, the work forest read off the initial serial-indexed table of the list is exactly the initial leaf forest of the list, in the same order.

results.title: Appending to the table appends to the forest
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every table $T$ whose cells each hold at most one work item and every work item $x$, the work forest of the table obtained from $T$ by appending a new last cell holding $x$ is the work forest of $T$ followed by $x$.

results.title: Heap of a Huffman work forest
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The heap of a list of Huffman work items is obtained from the empty binary min-heap by inserting the priorities of the items one at a time, in list order.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The loop takes a fuel $n$, a next serial number $s$, a binary min-heap $H$ of Huffman priorities, ordered lexicographically by weight and then serial number, and a table $T$ whose cells each hold at most one work item. Taking serial $i$ from a table succeeds when cell $i$ holds a work item whose priority has serial number $i$, and returns that item's tree together with the table with cell $i$ emptied. With fuel…

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The loop takes a fuel $n$, a next serial number $s$, a binary min-heap $H$ of Huffman priorities, ordered lexicographically by weight and then serial number, a table $T$ whose cells each hold at most one work item, and a counter $c$. Taking serial $i$ from a table succeeds when cell $i$ holds a work item whose priority has serial number $i$, and returns that item's tree together with the table with cell $i$…

results.title: Huffman loop with lookup count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a fuel $n$, a next serial number $s$, a binary min-heap $H$ of Huffman priorities and a table $T$ whose cells each hold at most one work item, the Huffman loop with lookup count on $(n, s, H, T)$ is the Huffman loop with an accumulated lookup count on $(n, s, H, T)$ started with counter $0$. It runs the bounded sequence of Huffman merges and counts indexed table lookups, one for each work item taken from the…

results.title: Lookup count of the instrumented Huffman loop
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every fuel $n$, next serial number $s$, binary min-heap $H$ of Huffman priorities and table $T$ whose cells each hold at most one work item, the Huffman loop with lookup count on $(n, s, H, T)$ fails exactly when the bounded Huffman merge loop on $(n, s, H, T)$ fails, and returns $(t, 2n + 1)$ when the merge loop returns the tree $t$: two indexed table reads for each of the $n$ merges and one for the final step.

results.title: Discarding the lookup count recovers the Huffman loop
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every fuel $n$, next serial number $s$, binary min-heap $H$ of Huffman priorities and table $T$ whose cells each hold at most one work item, discarding the count from the result of the Huffman loop with lookup count on $(n, s, H, T)$ gives the result of the bounded Huffman merge loop on $(n, s, H, T)$: the two fail together, and otherwise they return the same tree.

results.title: Indexed reads of a successful Huffman loop
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k$ be a merge budget, $n$ a next serial number, $h$ a binary min-heap of Huffman priorities and $t$ a serial-indexed table of optional Huffman work items. If the Huffman loop with budget $k$ on $n$, $h$ and $t$ returns a tree $T$, then the Huffman loop with lookup counting on the same arguments returns $T$ together with the count $2k + 1$ of indexed payload-table reads.

results.title: Huffman's algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a list of $n$ pairs $(a_0, w_0), \dots, (a_{n-1}, w_{n-1})$ of symbols and natural-number weights, with decidable equality on symbols. The construction fails when $L$ is empty or two pairs share a symbol. Otherwise it starts from $n$ leaves, the leaf for $(a_i, w_i)$ having priority (weight $w_i$, serial $i$), and performs $n - 1$ merges: each merge removes the two trees whose priorities are least in the…

results.title: Huffman's construction keeps the weighted leaves
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a list of pairs $(a, w)$ of a symbol $a$ and a natural-number weight $w$, with decidable equality on symbols. If the Huffman construction on $L$ succeeds with a tree $T$, then the list of weighted leaves of $T$, read left to right, is a permutation of $L$.

results.title: Huffman codes are prefix-free
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the Huffman construction succeeds on a list of weighted symbols and returns a tree $T$, then the code of $T$ on its leaf symbols is prefix-free: for any two distinct leaf symbols of $T$, neither codeword is a prefix of the other.

results.title: Huffman weight tree
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A Huffman weight tree is a full binary tree whose leaves carry only real weights: it is either a leaf with a weight $w \in \mathbb{R}$, or a fork joining a left and a right Huffman weight tree.

results.title: Multiset of leaf weights
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The leaf weights of a Huffman weight tree form a multiset of reals that forgets where the leaves sit: a leaf of weight $w$ gives $\{w\}$, and a tree with subtrees $L$ and $R$ gives the multiset sum of the leaf weights of $L$ and those of $R$.

results.title: Total leaf weight of a Huffman weight tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The total weight of a Huffman weight tree is the sum of its leaf weights: a leaf of weight $w$ has total weight $w$, and a tree with subtrees $L$ and $R$ has total weight equal to the total weight of $L$ plus that of $R$.

results.title: Weighted external path length of a Huffman weight tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Huffman weight tree $T$, write $w(T)$ for its total leaf weight. The weighted external path length $P(T)$ of $T$ is defined by the merge recurrence: a leaf $T$ has $P(T) = 0$, and a tree $T$ with subtrees $L$ and $R$ has $P(T) = P(L) + P(R) + w(L) + w(R)$.

results.title: Height of a weight tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The height of a weight tree is the number of edges on a longest path from the root to a leaf: a leaf has height $0$, and a fork with subtrees $L$ and $R$ has height $1 + \max(\mathrm{height}(L), \mathrm{height}(R))$.

results.title: Weight at a given depth
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: For a real number $v$, a weight tree $T$ and a natural number $d$, the relation "$T$ contains $v$ at depth $d$" is defined inductively: the leaf of weight $v$ contains $v$ at depth $0$, and if $L$ contains $v$ at depth $d$ or $R$ contains $v$ at depth $d$, then the fork with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ contains $v$ at depth $d + 1$. Thus it holds exactly when some leaf of $T$ of weight $v$ lies at depth…

results.title: Reweighting one leaf occurrence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Suppose a leaf of weight $v$ occurs at depth $d$ in a Huffman weight tree $T$, and let $r$ be a real number. Then there are a multiset $R$ of reals and a Huffman weight tree $T'$ such that the multiset of leaf weights of $T$ is $\{v\} + R$, that of $T'$ is $\{r\} + R$, the total leaf weight of $T'$ is that of $T$ plus $r - v$, the weighted external path length of $T'$ is that of $T$ plus $d(r - v)$, and $T'$ has…

results.title: Raising one leaf weight in a bounded-height tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a Huffman weight tree whose height is at most a natural number $B$, and write $W(T)$ for its multiset of leaf weights. Let $v \le r$ be real numbers and let $S$ be a multiset of reals with $\{r\} + W(T) = \{v\} + S$. Then there is a Huffman weight tree $T'$ with multiset of leaf weights $S$ and height at most $B$ whose weighted external path length is at most that of $T$ plus $B(r - v)$.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a Huffman weight tree whose height is at most a natural number $B$, and write $W(T)$ for its multiset of leaf weights. Let $f, s, \ell, n$ be real numbers with $\ell \le n$, $\ell \le f$ and $n \le s$, and let $S$ be a multiset of reals with $\{f, s\} + W(T) = \{\ell, n\} + S$. results.title: Contracting a deepest sibling pair
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a weight tree of height $h \ge 1$. Then there are real numbers $x$ and $y$, a multiset $M$ of real numbers and a real number $c$ such that the multiset of leaf weights of $T$ is $\{x, y\} + M$, the path cost of $T$ is $c + hx + hy$, and for every real number $z$ there is a weight tree $T'$ of height at most $h$ whose multiset of leaf weights is $\{z\} + M$ and whose path cost is $c + (h - 1)z$.

results.title: Contracting the two least weights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a weight tree, let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers and let $M$ be a multiset of real numbers such that the multiset of leaf weights of $T$ is $\{a, b\} + M$, $a \le b$, and $b \le w$ for every $w \in M$. Then there is a weight tree $T'$ whose multiset of leaf weights is $\{a + b\} + M$ and whose path cost satisfies $\mathrm{cost}(T') + a + b \le \mathrm{cost}(T)$, where $\mathrm{cost}$ denotes path cost.

results.title: Two-minimum merge trace
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: The relation "$c$ is a two-minimum merge cost of the multiset $W$ of real weights" is defined inductively by two rules. A singleton multiset $\{w\}$ has merge cost $0$. If $a \le b$, every element of the multiset $R$ is at least $b$, and $c$ is a merge cost of $\{a + b\} + R$, then $a + b + c$ is a merge cost of $\{a, b\} + R$. Thus a merge cost is the total cost of repeatedly replacing two smallest weights by…

results.title: Two-minimum merge costs lower-bound weighted path length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $W$ be a multiset of real weights and let $c$ be a merge cost of $W$ certified by a two-minimum merge trace. Then every Huffman weight tree whose multiset of leaf weights is $W$ has weighted external path length at least $c$.

results.title: Erasing symbols from a Huffman tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Erasing the symbols of a Huffman tree gives the weight tree of the same shape: a leaf with symbol $s$ and natural-number weight $w$ becomes the leaf of real weight $w$, and a fork with subtrees $L$ and $R$ becomes the fork whose subtrees are the erasures of $L$ and $R$.

results.title: Erasing symbols preserves leaf weights
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Huffman tree $T$, the multiset of leaf weights of the weight tree obtained from $T$ by erasing its symbols is the multiset of the weights $w$, viewed as real numbers, over the weighted leaves $(s, w)$ of $T$.

results.title: Erasing symbols preserves total weight
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Huffman tree $T$, the total weight of the weight tree obtained from $T$ by erasing its symbols equals the total weight of $T$, viewed as a real number.

results.title: Erasing symbols preserves weighted path length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Huffman tree $T$, the path cost of the weight tree obtained from $T$ by erasing its symbols equals the weighted path length of $T$, viewed as a real number.

results.title: Priorities of a Huffman work forest
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The priorities of a list of Huffman work items form the multiset consisting of the priority of each item in the list, counted with multiplicity.

results.title: Weights of a Huffman work forest
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The weights of a list of Huffman work items form the multiset consisting of the total leaf weight of each item's tree, taken as a real number, counted with multiplicity.

results.title: Cost of a Huffman work forest
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The cost of a list of Huffman work items is the real number obtained by summing, over the items in the list, the weighted path length of each item's tree.

results.summary: Let $L$ be a list of symbol–weight pairs with natural-number weights, over a symbol type with decidable equality, and suppose the Huffman construction returns the tree $t$ on $L$. results.title: Huffman's construction succeeds on nonempty inputs with distinct symbols
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a nonempty list of symbol–weight pairs with natural-number weights, over a symbol type with decidable equality. If no symbol occurs in $L$ more than once, then the Huffman construction returns a tree on $L$.

results.title: Huffman's construction fails exactly on empty or repeated-symbol inputs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a list of symbol–weight pairs with natural-number weights, over a symbol type with decidable equality. The Huffman construction returns no tree on $L$ if and only if $L$ is empty or some symbol occurs in $L$ more than once.

results.title: Admissible Huffman trees
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given an input list of symbols with natural-number weights, a Huffman tree is admissible for the input when its list of weighted leaves, read from left to right, is a permutation of the input list: the leaves of the tree carry exactly the input's (symbol, weight) pairs, with the same multiplicities.

results.title: Optimality of Huffman coding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a list of symbol–weight pairs with natural-number weights, over a symbol type with decidable equality, and suppose the Huffman construction returns the tree $t$ on $L$. Then every coding tree $t'$ (a full binary tree whose leaves carry symbols and weights) whose weighted leaves, listed left to right, form a permutation of $L$ has weighted path length at least that of $t$.

results.title: Huffman's algorithm minimizes the encoded length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a list of symbol–weight pairs with natural-number weights, over a symbol type with decidable equality, and suppose Huffman's algorithm returns the tree $t$ on $L$. Then every Huffman tree $t'$ that is admissible for $L$, that is, whose weighted leaves listed from left to right form a permutation of $L$, has encoded length at least that of $t$.

results.title: Smith's remoteness function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an impartial game $G$, the remoteness $R(p)$ of a position $p$ of $G$ is defined by well-founded recursion along moves; the options of $p$ are the positions reachable from $p$ in one move. results.title: Recursion for Smith's remoteness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be an impartial game, $p$ a position of $G$, and $R$ the set of remotenesses of the options of $p$ (the positions reachable from $p$ in one move). If $R$ contains an even number, the remoteness of $p$ is $1$ plus the least even element of $R$; otherwise, if $R$ is nonempty, it is $1$ plus the largest element of $R$; and if $R$ is empty, it is $0$.

results.title: Smith's remoteness vanishes at terminal positions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In an impartial game, the remoteness of a terminal position (a position with no moves) is $0$.
